# Introduction

## Statement of the Problem

The general problem of this study is the performance degradation caused by negative transfer during the joint training of mixed-granularity tasks on code-switched Taglish disaster tweets.

The specific questions are the following:

1. How do single-task baselines perform on the three disaster triage tasks within each linguistic stratum on unseen typhoon events? *(Baseline Analysis)*

2. How can a Taglish dataset for disaster triage be constructed to support a controlled evaluation of multi-task training methods? *(Design & Artifact Creation)*

3. How does the multi-task model compare to the single-task baselines in inference efficiency on unseen typhoon events? *(Empirical Benchmarking)*

4. Is there a statistically significant difference in negative transfer among the five multi-task training methods on unseen typhoon events? *(Comparative Validation)*

## Objectives

The general objective of this study is to determine which multi-task training method best mitigates negative transfer in the joint training of disaster triage tasks on code-switched Taglish disaster tweets.

The specific objectives are the following:

1. To evaluate the performance of single-task baselines on the three disaster triage tasks within each linguistic stratum on unseen typhoon events. *(Baseline Analysis)*

2. To construct a Taglish dataset for disaster triage that supports a controlled evaluation of multi-task training methods. *(Design & Artifact Creation)*

3. To compare the inference efficiency of the multi-task model and the single-task baselines on unseen typhoon events. *(Empirical Benchmarking)*

4. To determine whether a statistically significant difference in negative transfer exists among the five multi-task training methods on unseen typhoon events. *(Comparative Validation)*

## Hypotheses

The five multi-task training methods evaluated are equal weighting, tuned static weighting, loss balancing (GradNorm), gradient surgery (PCGrad), and loss balancing with gradient surgery (GradNorm with PCGrad).

**Null Hypothesis ($H_0$).** There is no statistically significant difference in negative transfer among the five training methods on unseen typhoon events.

**Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$).** At least one of the five training methods differs significantly in negative transfer from at least one of the others on unseen typhoon events.
